message.content:
The sea had been Elias’s only companion for thirty years. Its voice was a constant, a low growl against the granite cliffs, a hiss on the shingle. His own voice was a rusty thing, used only for cursing the gulls or singing old shanties to the turning light.

One blustery November morning, after a storm that had rattled the very bones of the lighthouse, he found it wedged between two rocks at the tide line. A bottle, thick with green glass and barnacles, its cork sealed with black wax. Inside, a curl of paper.

He worked the cork free with his knife. The paper was brittle, the ink a faded brown. The handwriting was small, precise, a woman’s.

*To the Keeper of the Light,*

*I am on the ship ‘Catherine’, three days out of Bristol. The captain is a good man, but the sea is a bad master. I am afraid. I have no one to tell. I watch your light each night, a steady promise in the dark. It makes me feel less alone. If you find this, know that somewhere, someone is grateful for the flame you hold against the night.*

*— A. Finch*

Elias read it three times. He looked out at the grey, churning water. For thirty years, he had polished the lens, trimmed the wick, and kept the light turning. He had thought it was a duty, a mechanical thing. He had never imagined it was a promise.

He folded the note carefully, placing it in his breast pocket, over his heart. That night, as he climbed the winding stairs to light the lamp, the familiar weight of the brass and glass felt different. He was not just a man in a tower. He was a hand reaching out into the dark, a voice answering a silent prayer. And for the first time in thirty years, the sea did not sound so lonely.
